content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-marketplace/superpowers/7.0.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

Update from Claude, an agent working under Rod's direction: the overnight
flags are now measured on the board. These are profile builds of
`feature/43-gl-speed-experiments`, pinned with rotation off, flashed with
`tools/ab_flash.py`. Each variant ran two rounds of 60 s, and the rounds agreed
to within 0.05 ms.

## Lazy lighting: a real, modest gain, now the default on the branch

| Hack | Before | `GL_LAZY_SHADE` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gears (boot layout, 4,298 vertices) | 61.1 ms, 13.8 fps | 57.7 ms, 14.5 fps |
| Morph3D | 61.4 ms, 13.9 fps | 58.4 ms, 14.4 fps |
| CubicGrid (points, unlit) | 47.9 ms | 47.9 ms |

It is on by default on the branch now (`8138ef3`); `-DGL_EAGER_SHADE` turns it
off. All 520 host tests pass, and every pinned frame hash is unchanged.

## Memory placement barely matters

On Gears, against the profile-only build:

- `GL_IRAM`: 0.7 ms slower.
- `GL_INTERNAL_MATRICES`: no change.
- `PSRAM_AUTOLOAD=1` (prefetch on a miss): no change. `=3` (hit and miss):
  0.8 ms faster.

The first autoload build boot-looped on the watchdog: its region covered the
whole 32 MB data bus, so a prefetch reached unmapped pages and the panic
handler faulted too. It now covers mapped PSRAM only (`7d0bfa6`).

## Where a frame goes

Gears' frame, from the `glprof` line (the stages nest):

- Fill: 28 ms, about 47% of the frame, for about 1,600 triangles of about 30
  pixels each.
- Vertex work outside lighting: about 17 ms, roughly 4 us a vertex.
- Clear: 6 ms.
- Lighting: 3.7 ms. That is why lazy lighting saves no more on this layout.

CubicGrid: 8,000 points at about 1.45 us each (11.6 ms), a 12 ms clear, and a
32 ms full-screen push.

## Why fill is slow: PSRAM cache misses

A boot-time benchmark in `GL_PROFILE` builds measures, per access to a new
32-byte line:

| Access | Cycles |
| --- | --- |
| PSRAM read | 129 (0.54 us) |
| PSRAM read-modify-write | 220 (0.92 us), the extra being the dirty-line write-back |
| Lines in address order vs a row apart | the same, so no prefetch benefit |
| Internal RAM, loop included | 17 |

Each row of a small triangle touches new lines in both the z-buffer and the
canvas. At roughly 16 lines a triangle, that comes to about 23 of the 28 ms.
The Arduino SDK fixes the data cache at 32 KB with 32-byte lines and PSRAM at
80 MHz octal. The S3 can do a 64 KB cache and 64-byte lines, but only with a
rebuilt SDK.

## Next

Rod has agreed to design a banded renderer:

- transform each vertex once
- sort the screen-space triangles into horizontal bands
- rasterise each band against a z-buffer and colour band held in internal RAM
- copy each band out

The aim is to take most of fill and clear (about 34 ms on Gears) out of PSRAM.
Separately, the `GL_LINE_LOOP`/`GL_POLYGON` overrun guard is in draft PR #79.

Issues #43 and #44 · night of 10 to 11 October 2026

TinyGL overnight report

Rod, here is what I tried on GL speed and Pipes while you slept, what I learned, and what I'd like to flash first. Nothing has touched the board: every number here is from the host or from the device build, and the board estimates are labelled as estimates.

The short version

Best lead

Lazy lighting (GL_LAZY_SHADE): TinyGL lights every vertex before back-face culling throws most of them away. Lighting only what gets drawn halves the lighting work in Gears' heavy layout, and every frame hash is identical.

Tool

One-flash profile (GL_PROFILE): cycle counts per stage printed next to each run line, so a single capture gives the whole breakdown instead of one flash per early return.

Pipes

An exact incremental redraw works on the host (about 300 vertices a frame instead of up to 977,000). But Pipes as written needs about 22 MB of display lists, and the board has about 7 MB free. It can fit with smaller screens and a fixed camera.

Bug

TinyGL here draws no GL_LINE_LOOPs, so StonerView's square outlines have never shown, and a loop or polygon of more than four vertices overwrote the GL context. I fixed the overwrite; whether to draw the outlines is your call.

What I learned about where the time goes

  • It isn't soft-float any more. I disassembled the device build. The vertex and triangle path calls only ROM __divsf3 (a 48-byte FPU routine) and newlib sqrtf. Software double shows up only on the specular and positional-light paths, which no ported hack uses. GCC 8.4 won't inline sqrtf or a divide, even with -fno-math-errno.
  • The hot code is small. A per-frame call profile on the host, mapped onto the device function sizes, comes to about 6 KB of code for Gears' heavy layout and 3 KB for CubicGrid. The instruction cache is 16 KB, so flash-cache misses are probably not the main cost.
  • The data side is the likelier suspect. Display lists are PSRAM reads of 20 to 52 bytes a vertex (a glColor op alone is 32 bytes), and the z-buffer and canvas are PSRAM too, behind a 32 KB data cache with 32-byte lines. The lists can't move to internal RAM: Gears' heavy layout reads about 420 KB of list ops a frame.
  • Culling discards most of the lighting. Gears' heavy layout submits 17,624 triangles and fills 5,330, but lights all 17,700 vertices first. That is what lazy lighting goes after.
----

What I'd like to flash, in order

  1. GL_PROFILE alone, pinned to Gears (first layout), then CubicGrid. One capture each gives the stage breakdown that everything else should be judged against.
  2. Lazy lighting A/B on Gears and Morph3D. If the board agrees with the host, I'd propose it as the default.
  3. GL_IRAM, GL_INTERNAL_MATRICES, PSRAM_AUTOLOAD=1, one at a time, keeping only what moves step.
  4. Then, depending on the profile, the bigger moves: running the panel flush on core 0 while the next frame starts (it reads M5GFX's buffer, not the canvas, but releasing the SPI bus from another task needs care), or rasterising on core 0 while core 1 transforms.

Both are in the numbers already, and they point the same way as Gears, only harder.

**What I know so far:**
- **Hypnowheel** runs at 1.4 fps (720 ms a frame). It was dropped from the rotation (#73).
  - **Blended fill, about 70%:** about 435,000 additively blended pixels a frame at about 1.2 µs each. That's roughly 290 cycles a pixel, and every one is a read-modify-write of the canvas in PSRAM.
  - **Triangle setup, about 30%:** about 5,900 triangles at about 35 µs each. My guess is that a fair share of that is PSRAM misses too.
- **Unknown Pleasures** runs at about 5 fps (about 165 ms a frame). It draws filled quads plus smoothed lines, with the depth test and polygon offset. I don't yet have a stage breakdown for it.

**My guess at what banding would buy:**
- **Hypnowheel:** with the blend done in internal RAM, at a few tens of cycles a pixel instead of about 290, it might go from 720 ms to somewhere around 150 to 250 ms. That's 4 to 6 fps: much better, but still nowhere near 15.
- **Unknown Pleasures:** probably a similar proportional gain, but I'd want its profile before guessing a number.

The design differs for these two. Big blended triangles span many bands, and blending needs the existing canvas pixels in each band, not just a cleared one.

I'd like to measure both on the board before designing:
1. Merge current `main` into the experiments branch.
2. Flash a `GL_PROFILE` build pinned to Unknown Pleasures.
3. Flash one pinned to Hypnowheel, registered only in that temporary build.

That gives a stage-by-stage breakdown for each, and a measured cost of a blended pixel against an opaque one.

content.text:
Here's what the board says about your three, and what it means for the design.

| Hack | Now | Where the time goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown Pleasures | 4.7 fps, 174 ms step | fill 69 ms, triangle setup 40 ms, smooth lines 30 ms, clear 25 ms; push 32 ms + 11 ms sync |
| Hypnowheel | 1.4 fps, 706 ms step | fill 358 ms, setup 61 ms, clear 12 ms, **about 275 ms in the hack's own `double` trig** |
| Pipes (host lab only) | not on the board | vertices and lighting, not fill |

**What that means:**
- **Hypnowheel has a cheap first win that isn't GL at all.** A single-precision wrapper, the same trick as Galaxy and Substrate with the hack left byte-identical, should take out most of the 275 ms. That's my estimate; I haven't built it yet.
- **Banding is aimed at fill, clear and lines.** That's about 165 ms of Unknown Pleasures' 174 ms and about 370 ms of Hypnowheel's. If rasterising in internal RAM costs a quarter of what it does in PSRAM, my guess is:
  - Unknown Pleasures: 174 → roughly 80 ms (about 9 fps with the push).
  - Hypnowheel: after the trig fix, roughly 150 ms (about 5 fps).
- **Pipes wants something different.** With a fixed camera, the incremental redraw already makes steady frames tiny; the fade is vertex-bound, which lazy lighting helps.
- **One clash to design around:** the incremental redraw needs the full z-buffer and canvas kept from the last frame. A banded renderer with z-buffer bands in internal RAM throws those away, so Pipes would either stay on the normal path or bands would have to be saved back.

So my guess is this is really three pieces of work:
1. Hypnowheel's trig.
2. The banded renderer, for Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel.
3. A Pipes port using the incremental redraw.

The banded renderer is the only big one.

What's wrong or missing in that? And for the banded renderer: must frames come out pixel-identical to today's, so every pinned frame hash still matches, or would you accept small differences for speed?
Issue 73 was also related to Hypnowheel performance, so might offer some ideas.  Pixel-identical isn't important. Small differences are fine.
I'll check #73's comments for anything beyond the two ideas in its body:

content.text:
#73 has no comments, but its body offers two ideas. Both fit now that pixel-identical isn't required:

1. **A faster additive blend.** The canvas is RGB565, so a saturating add can do two pixels at once with bit masks, instead of TinyGL's per-pixel decode and re-encode. That suits Hypnowheel's `GL_ONE, GL_ONE` fill.
2. **Render at half resolution and scale up**, as Fireworkx already does through `lowrez_put.h`. That's a quarter of the pixels.

There's a bonus with the second: at 233×233 the z-buffer is 108 KB, which might fit in internal RAM whole, with no bands needed. It would soften edges, though. That's fine for Hypnowheel's broad spirals, but I'd expect it to spoil Unknown Pleasures, whose look is its thin smoothed lines.

**My play-back of the design so far:**
- **Goal:** make Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel much faster. Pipes is a separate piece of work, built on the incremental redraw.
- **Exactness:** not required, so the pinned frame hashes can be re-pinned. I'd still want a test that compares banded frames with today's and fails on large differences.
- **Mechanism:**
  1. Transform each vertex once.
  2. Sort the screen-space triangles and lines into horizontal bands.
  3. Rasterise each band against a z-buffer and colour band in internal RAM.
  4. Copy each finished band out to the canvas.
  - Clearing becomes nearly free, because each band starts as the clear colour in fast memory.
- **Riding along in the same fast inner loop, my additions:** the two-pixel blend from #73 and quicker smooth lines.
- **Separate and first:** Hypnowheel's single-precision wrapper, since it's unrelated to rendering and cheap.
- **Half resolution:** kept as a per-hack option. My guess is it's for Hypnowheel only, and it needs your eye on the look.

What's wrong or missing there? And should banding be something each GL hack opts into, the way Unknown Pleasures opts into synced pushes, or the one path every GL hack goes through?
Would there be a downside to it being the one path?
A few, mostly at the edges. Before answering, I'm checking which of our GL hacks clear the screen every frame, because that's where the downsides live:

content.text:
Not for the hacks we have. Every registered GL hack clears the screen each frame, and none uses textures or reads pixels back, so all of them fit the banded model cleanly. The downsides are real, but they all have the same answer, an automatic fallback:

1. **Frames that build on the last one.** A band starts life in fast memory as the clear colour. A frame that doesn't begin with a clear, like Pipes' incremental redraw, would need each band loaded from the PSRAM canvas and z-buffer and written back. That's slower than today's direct path. The renderer can see whether a frame started with a clear and draw directly when it didn't.
2. **Very large frames.** Every triangle is held until the frame ends, so the holding area needs a cap: Pipes' fade alone is about 977,000 vertices. If a frame overflows it, the renderer has to fall back for the rest of that frame, or flush part-way.
3. **Mid-frame state changes.** Each held triangle has to remember the blend mode, depth test, polygon offset and shading in force when it was drawn. That's more memory and more code to get right. Unknown Pleasures switches between filled quads and lines with an offset within one frame, so this matters from day one.
4. **Internal RAM.** Bands plus the holding area might want 60 to 120 KB of the roughly 305 KB free. Today that's fine, but it's taken from every hack, GL or not, unless it's only allocated while a GL hack runs. I'd allocate it only then.
5. **Simple scenes gain little.** CubicGrid's points and Morph3D's small object would pay the sorting cost for a small saving. I'd guess they still come out about even or ahead.
6. **One bug hits every GL hack at once.** It's mitigated by the frame comparison tests, but a bug would show everywhere rather than in one hack.

The upside of one path is a single thing to test and maintain, and every GL hack, including future ports, gets faster without anyone deciding per hack.

So my recommendation: one path, falling back to today's direct drawing for frames that don't start with a clear and for frames that overflow. That keeps Pipes' incremental redraw working unchanged.

Does one path with that automatic fallback sound right to you?

The experiments branch now has current `main` merged in. It passes all 558 host tests and is pushed; GitHub rejected the first push and accepted the retry.

My question still stands: does one rendering path for every GL hack, falling back to today's direct drawing for frames that don't start with a clear or overflow the holding area, sound right to you?
Yes, one path with the fallback sounds right

Good. Here's the play-back of how it would behave, with my calls marked as mine:

- **When:** a frame that starts with `glClear` of colour and depth is held. Every triangle, line and point is transformed and lit as now, then stored with its screen position, colours, depth, and the state in force at the time (blend, depth test, offset, shading).
- **At the swap:** each band is cleared to the clear colour and depth in internal RAM. All stored primitives that touch the band are rasterised, and the band is copied to the canvas. Only rows inside the dirty box get copied, so the existing push logic is untouched.
- **Fallback:** a frame that doesn't start with a clear, or that overflows the holding area, draws straight to the canvas as today. Pipes' incremental redraw relies on that.
- **Memory (my call):** bands and the holding area are allocated when a GL hack starts and freed when it stops, so non-GL hacks lose nothing. Band height comes from what fits in internal RAM, probably 32 to 64 rows.

# Banded GL renderer: design

Issue #43. Agreed with Rod on 2026-10-11. This document is a planning
artefact: it lives on the feature branch and does not merge to `main`.

## Why

Rod wants Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel to run visibly faster on the
StopWatch. Hypnowheel was dropped from the rotation at 1.4 fps (issue #73).
Success is judged by Rod watching the board ("I know it when I see it"), not
by an fps target, so the work must stop at points where he can look.

Board profiles (`GL_PROFILE` builds of `feature/43-gl-speed-experiments`,
pinned, rotation off; stage times nest):

| Hack | Step | Fill | Triangle setup outside fill | Lines | Clear | Other |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown Pleasures | 174 ms | 69 ms (5,442 tris) | 40 ms | 30 ms (3,960) | 25 ms | push 32 ms + 11 ms sync |
| Hypnowheel | 706 ms | 358 ms (5,949 tris) | 61 ms | 0 | 12 ms | about 275 ms in the hack's `double` trig |
| Gears (boot layout) | 58 ms with lazy lighting | 28 ms (1,600 tris) | 2 ms | 0 | 6 ms | vertex work about 17 ms |

The cause of slow fill is PSRAM. A boot benchmark measured a new 32-byte PSRAM
cache line at 129 cycles to read and about 220 to read and write back, against
17 for internal RAM. Lines a row apart cost the same as lines in address
order, so hardware prefetch cannot help (measured: `PSRAM_AUTOLOAD` changed
Gears by under 1 ms). A small triangle touches new z-buffer and canvas lines on
every row. The Arduino SDK fixes the data cache at 32 KB with 32-byte lines.

The fix is to rasterise into internal RAM: hold a frame's primitives, then
draw the screen in horizontal bands whose colour and depth live in internal
RAM, copying each finished band to the canvas.

## Goals

- Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel visibly faster on the board, with Rod
  looking at each step.
- One rendering path for every GL hack, with an automatic fallback (below).
  No per-hack flag decides whether a hack is banded.
- Every registered GL hack keeps working and looks the same to the eye:
  Gears, Morph3D, CubicGrid, StonerView, Unknown Pleasures, HexTrail.

## Non-goals

- Pixel-identical output. Rod accepts small differences, so the pinned frame
  hashes in `test_hacks.c` will be re-pinned.
- Pipes. It is a separate piece of work built on the incremental redraw in
  `docs/pipes-lab/` (branch `feature/44-pipes`). This design must not break
  that redraw, and the fallback is what protects it.
- Vertex and lighting cost. Lazy lighting already landed on the experiments
  branch; per-vertex work is left alone here.
- Moving the push to the other core, a 64 KB data cache, or a faster PSRAM
  clock.

## Anti-goals

- A slower frame for any registered GL hack. The fallback exists so that
  frames the banded path cannot help draw as they do today.
- Taking internal RAM from non-GL hacks. Band memory is allocated only while
  a GL hack runs.
- Editing copied hacks. They stay byte-identical (AGENTS.md).

## Constraints

- ESP32-S3, 240 MHz. About 305 KB of internal heap is free while a GL hack
  runs (`heap=` in the `run` line). Canvas, z-buffer and display lists are in
  PSRAM (about 6 MB free).
- The canvas is 466 by 466 RGB565 with bytes swapped (display order). TinyGL
  draws straight into `canvas->px`, and the z-buffer is 16-bit.
- TinyGL under `firmware/src/tinygl/` stays byte-identical. All changes go
  through `tools/tinygl_patch.py` (checked anchors) or `firmware/src/glshim/`.
- The dirty-rectangle contract (`.claude/rules/gl.md`): TinyGL reports the box
  around what it draws to `glshim_note_box`, `glClear` clears only the box
  drawn since the last clear, and a swap marks only what was drawn and erased.
  Nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs.
- Behaviour already patched into TinyGL must survive banding: polygon offset
  with its snapping margin, smooth (Wu) lines with fractional endpoints,
  `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` treated as opaque, additive blending, the
  depth clear skipped while the depth test is off, and lazy lighting.
- Host tests first, under AddressSanitizer; mutation-check new tests.
- Rod has given standing permission to flash for this session. Report
  "compiles", "host tests pass" and "runs on the device" separately.

## Decided

### Order of work

1. **Hypnowheel's trig, first and separately.** A single-precision wrapper for
   Hypnowheel, like Galaxy and Substrate (`.claude/skills/port-hack/`,
   "Single precision"). The hack stays byte-identical. Profile it on the board,
   which needs a temporary registry entry, as Hypnowheel is not registered.
   Rod looks.
1. **The banded renderer**, below. Profile Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel,
   and A/B every registered GL hack against the experiments branch with
   `tools/ab_flash.py`. Rod looks.
1. **Half resolution for Hypnowheel, as an option.** Render its GL frame at
   233 by 233 and scale up (as `hacks/lowrez_put.h` does for Fireworkx). Flash
   it and the full-resolution build pinned, and give Rod the numbers side by
   side; he chooses. Not for Unknown Pleasures, whose look is its thin lines.
1. **Whether Hypnowheel goes back into the rotation** is Rod's call after he
   has seen it.

### How a frame is drawn

- **Held frames.** A frame is held when it begins with a `glClear` of both the
  colour and the depth buffer (or of the colour buffer with the depth test
  off). From then until the swap, each triangle, line and point is transformed
  and lit as now and then stored, not drawn. A stored primitive keeps its
  screen-space vertices (`ZBufferPoint`, including the fractional line
  positions), its kind, and the state that affects rasterising: blend on and
  its function, depth test, depth write, polygon offset, shade model, smooth
  lines, and the dirty-box margin rule.
- **At the swap** (`glXSwapBuffers`, and any call that must see the pixels),
  the screen is drawn band by band. Each band starts in internal RAM as the
  clear colour and clear depth, gets every stored primitive that touches its
  rows, and is then copied to the canvas. Only rows inside the dirty box are
  copied; the dirty-box bookkeeping and the push are unchanged.
- **Fallback.** A frame draws straight to the canvas, as today, when it does
  not begin with such a clear (Pipes' incremental redraw), or when the store
  fills up. On overflow, the rest of the frame falls back. The builder may
  instead flush part-way, provided the result is correct.
- **Memory.** The bands and the store are allocated when a GL context opens
  and freed when it closes (`glshim_open`, and the release hook).
- **Inner loops.** The band rasteriser includes the two-pixel additive blend
  from issue #73 (a saturating RGB565 add with masks, two pixels per 32-bit
  word) and smooth lines that write to the band.

### Tests

- Banded frames compared with direct-drawn frames of the same scene on the
  host, within a small tolerance. The tolerance must be tight enough that a
  band seam, a missing band or a lost primitive fails.
- Exact tests for each fallback case: no clear, colour-only clear, store
  overflow.
- Tests for each state a stored primitive carries (blend, offset, depth test
  off, smooth lines), since each changes on the fly in Unknown Pleasures.
- Re-pin the frame hashes in `test_hacks.c` once the banded output is right,
  then check every GL hack on the board.

## Left to the builder

- Band height, from what fits in the internal RAM left over (probably 32 to
  64 rows), and whether bands are rows of the whole canvas or of the dirty box.
- The store's layout and size cap, and whether it lives in internal RAM or
  PSRAM (written once and read once per band, so sequential).
- How primitives are binned to bands (a list per band, or a sorted pass).
- How the rasterisers are limited to a band's rows: patching `ztriangle.h`'s
  row loop through `tinygl_patch.py`, or a `ZBuffer` whose `pbuf` and `zbuf`
  point at the band with a y offset.
- Whether points get their own fast path.
- Which calls besides the swap force the held frame out (`glFinish`,
  `glDrawPixels`, text drawing, a context change).

## Risks

- The estimate is rough. If rasterising in internal RAM costs a quarter of what
  it costs in PSRAM, Unknown Pleasures goes from 174 ms to roughly 80 ms and
  Hypnowheel, after its trig fix, to roughly 150 ms. Neither is measured.
- Triangle setup is repeated for each band a triangle touches. Hypnowheel's
  large triangles span many bands, and setup was already 61 ms.
- Unknown Pleasures switches between filled quads and lines with an offset
  within a frame, so a state-capture bug would show there first.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

# Banded GL Renderer Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use
> superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or
> superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use
> checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Make Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel visibly faster on the board by
rasterising GL frames in horizontal bands held in internal RAM.

**Architecture:** A frame that starts with a qualifying `glClear` is held:
TinyGL still clips, culls, lights and offsets as now, but where it would call
a rasteriser (`ZB_fillTriangle*`, `ZB_line*`, `ZB_plot`) it stores the call
instead. At the swap each band of rows is cleared in internal RAM, every
stored call that touches it is replayed through the same rasteriser against
a band-sized `ZBuffer`, and the band is copied to the canvas. Anything the
held path cannot take spills: the held calls are drawn out (colour and depth)
and the rest of the frame draws directly.

**Tech Stack:** C (TinyGL patched by `tools/tinygl_patch.py`), `glshim`,
PlatformIO (`native` Unity tests under AddressSanitizer, `stopwatch` board
build), Python 3.13 with pytest for the patch tests, `tools/ab_flash.py` for
board A/B runs.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-11-banded-renderer-design.md`

## Global Constraints

- Copied hacks stay byte-identical; TinyGL under `firmware/src/tinygl/` stays
  byte-identical. Change TinyGL only through `tools/tinygl_patch.py` with
  checked anchors (add a test in `tools/tests/test_tinygl_patch.py` for each).
- Test first, on the host; mutation-check every new test (AGENTS.md).
- One path for every GL hack; the only per-hack switch is
  `glshim_set_banding(0)`, for hacks that draw against earlier frames' depth
  (Pipes' wrapper).
- Band memory is allocated only while a GL context is open.
- No GL hack may get slower: A/B every registered GL hack on the board
  (Gears, Morph3D, CubicGrid, StonerView, Unknown Pleasures, HexTrail).
- Report "compiles", "host tests pass" and "runs on the device" separately.
  Rod judges the look; stop for him where a task says so.
- Commits: named paths with `git add`, never `-A`; end with
  `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
- Work on `feature/43-banded-renderer` (branched from
  `feature/43-gl-speed-experiments`, which has `GL_PROFILE`, lazy lighting and
  `tools/ab_flash.py`). Planning docs do not merge to `main`.
- Board numbers to beat (profile builds, lazy lighting on): Unknown Pleasures
  174 ms step; Hypnowheel 706 ms; Gears boot layout 57.7 ms; Morph3D 58.4 ms;
  CubicGrid 47.9 ms.

## Review Focus

1. A frame that clears colour only, with the depth test on, after a held
   frame: the PSRAM z-buffer is stale. Expect the context to stop banding for
   good from that frame on, so later frames match the direct path (Task 3).
1. Internal RAM unavailable at `glshim_open`: expect banding to stay off and
   every frame to draw directly, never a crash (Task 3).
1. A hack stopped between its clear and its swap (rotation or a button
   press): expect the held calls to be dropped at close, and the next hack's
   first swap to replay nothing (Task 3).
1. Text drawn into a held frame (`ztext.c` writes `pbuf` directly): expect a
   spill first, so the text lands over what was drawn before it (Task 3).
1. Opening and closing a context many times: expect no growth in allocated
   bytes (Task 3).

---

### Task 1: Hypnowheel in single precision

**Files:**

- Create: `firmware/src/hacks/hypnowheel_single_gl.c`
- Modify: `firmware/src/hacks/registry.c` (entry under `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`)

  literals that `nm` shows as soft-double helpers)

**Interfaces:**

- Produces: `hypnowheel_hack`, registered last in `g_hacks[]` only when built

  unchanged.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the wrapper.** Model it on `hextrail_single_gl.c`:

- [ ] **Step 2: Register it under the flag.** Use the overrides it had before

- [ ] **Step 3: Check for soft-double helpers.** Compile the wrapper with

- [ ] **Step 4: Compare frames on the host.** Build `-e dump` with

- [ ] **Step 5: Run the full host suite.**

- [ ] **Step 6: Profile on the board.**

### Task 2: Rasterisers that stay inside a band

**Files:**

- Modify: `tools/tinygl_patch.py` (three new `Replace` entries)
- Test: `tools/tests/test_tinygl_patch.py`
- Create: `firmware/test/test_glshim_band/test_glshim_band.c`

**Interfaces:**

- Produces: every rasteriser draws only rows `0 <= y < zb->ysize`, whatever
  the `ZBufferPoint` y values (they may be negative or past the end). Task 3
  relies on this: it translates points by the band's first row and sets
  `ysize` to the band height.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests** in `test_glshim_band.c`. Each opens a
  `ZBuffer` with `ZB_open(64, 8, ZB_MODE_5R6G5B, rows)` over a 64 by 24 buffer
  whose middle 8 rows are the band, and the 8 rows either side are guards
  filled with a sentinel:
  - `test_a_triangle_taller_than_the_band_fills_only_band_rows`: points at
    y = -5, 3 and 14, filled with `ZB_fillTriangleSmoothNOBLEND`. Assert each
    band row has drawn pixels and every guard pixel still holds the sentinel.
  - `test_a_triangle_wholly_below_the_band_draws_nothing`: y = 9, 12, 15.
  - `test_a_line_crossing_the_band_draws_only_inside_it`: `ZB_line_z` from
    (2, -6) to (60, 13), and the same check with smooth lines on
    (`zb->line_smooth = 1`).
  - `test_a_point_outside_the_band_draws_nothing`: `ZB_plot` at y = -1 and
    y = 8, pointsize 1 and 3.
- [ ] **Step 2: Run them and watch them fail.**
  Run: `pio test -e native -f test_glshim_band`.
  Expected: guard pixels overwritten, or AddressSanitizer reports.
- [ ] **Step 3: Patch the three rasterisers** through `tinygl_patch.py`:
  - `src/ztriangle.h`: keep a row counter from `p0->y`; skip the span draw
    while it is below 0 and leave both parts once it reaches `zb->ysize`.
    Edge stepping continues as now, so pixels inside the band are unchanged.
  - `src/zline.h`: `PUTPIXEL` draws only when `pp` lies within
    `[zb->pbuf, zb->pbuf + zb->ysize * zb->linesize)`.
  - `src/zline.c` `ZB_plot`: skip any pixel with y outside `[0, zb->ysize)`.
  `zb_aa_plot` already checks bounds.
- [ ] **Step 4: Add patch tests** in `test_tinygl_patch.py` asserting each new
  text is present in the patched tree, as the existing tests do.
- [ ] **Step 5: Run everything.** `pio test -e native` and
  `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`. Expected: all pass,
  and every pinned frame hash in `test_hacks.c` unchanged.
- [ ] **Step 6: Mutation-check:** remove each of the three guards in turn and
  watch its test fail (scratchpad script, per AGENTS.md).
- [ ] **Step 7: Commit.**

### Task 3: Held frames for triangles, with spill and fallback

**Files:**

- Create: `firmware/src/glshim/glshim_band.h`, `firmware/src/glshim/glshim_band.c`
- Modify: `firmware/src/glshim/glshim.c` (clear, swap, open, close)
- Modify: `firmware/src/glshim/glshim.h` (`glshim_set_banding`)
- Modify: `tools/tinygl_patch.py` (fill call sites in `clip.c`; text and
  `glDrawPixels` spill)
- Test: `firmware/test/test_glshim_band/test_glshim_band.c`,
  `tools/tests/test_tinygl_patch.py`

**Interfaces:**

- Consumes: Task 2's band-safe rasterisers.
- Produces (in `glshim_band.h`):

```c
typedef void (*GlshimFillFn)(ZBuffer *, ZBufferPoint *, ZBufferPoint *,
                             ZBufferPoint *);
int glshim_band_open(int w, int h);  /* 0, or -1 if internal RAM is short */
void glshim_band_close(void);        /* drops any held calls */
void glshim_band_begin(ZBuffer *zb, PIXEL clear_color, GLint clear_z);
int glshim_band_holding(void);
int glshim_band_fill(ZBuffer *zb, GlshimFillFn fn, ZBufferPoint *a,
                     ZBufferPoint *b, ZBufferPoint *c); /* 1 if held */
void glshim_band_spill(ZBuffer *zb);  /* draw held calls, colour and depth */
void glshim_band_finish(ZBuffer *zb, int x0, int y0, int x1, int y1);
void glshim_band_set_capacity(int records); /* tests only */
```

- Produces (in `glshim.h`): `void glshim_set_banding(int on);`, 1 by default,
  reset to 1 by `glshim_close`. Pipes' wrapper will call it with 0.

Decisions the implementer must follow:

- **Record:** 64 bytes on the board. A 4-byte header (kind, rasteriser
  index into a table of the `ZB_fillTriangle*` functions, state index) and
  three vertices of `x`, `y` (int16), `z`, `r`, `g`, `b` (int32). Add
  `_Static_assert(sizeof(GlshimRecord) == 64)` under `__XTENSA__`. A texture
  fill, or any rasteriser not in the table, spills.
- **State table:** the `ZBuffer` fields a rasteriser reads (`enable_blend`,
  `sfactor`, `dfactor`, `blendeq`, `depth_test`, `depth_write`,
  `line_smooth`, `pointsize`), up to 255 distinct states a frame, a new entry
  only when the state differs from the last. Overflow spills. Because records
  are taken after the fill wrapper in `tinygl_patch.py`, the opaque
  `SRC_ALPHA` case and the polygon offset are already applied to what is
  stored.
- **Where things live:** records in PSRAM (`heap_caps_malloc` with
  `MALLOC_CAP_SPIRAM` on the board, `malloc` on the host), capacity 16,384
  (1 MB). A table of each record's first and last row (two `uint16_t`) in
  internal RAM (64 KB). One band of colour and depth, `GLSHIM_BAND_ROWS` = 32
  rows by the canvas width (about 60 KB), in internal RAM
  (`MALLOC_CAP_INTERNAL | MALLOC_CAP_8BIT`). If either internal allocation
  fails, `glshim_band_open` returns -1 and banding stays off.
- **Held frames:** `glshim_clear` calls `glshim_band_begin` instead of filling
  when banding is on and the clear covers colour and depth, or colour with the
  depth test off. It still adds the erased box to the swap's dirty box, and
  sets `g_z_valid = false`, because a held frame never writes the PSRAM
  z-buffer.
- **Replay:** for each band that the box `(x0, y0)` to `(x1, y1)` (this
  frame's drawn box joined with the erased box) touches, fill the band with
  the clear colour and depth. Replay, in order, every record whose row range
  meets the band, with y values moved up by the band's first row, through a
  `ZBuffer` copy whose `pbuf`, `zbuf` and `ysize` are the band's. Then copy
  the band's rows inside the box, columns `x0` to `x1`, to the canvas.
- **Spill:** replays the same way, but over the whole canvas box that a
  direct clear would have cleared plus the drawn box, and copies depth as
  well as colour to the PSRAM z-buffer. Then the frame continues directly.
  Spill on: a full store, a full state table, an unknown rasteriser, a text
  pixel (`ztext.c`) or `glDrawPixels`, and lines or points (until Task 4).
- **Sticky fallback:** when a frame draws with the depth test on but without
  a depth clear after a held frame, call `glshim_set_banding(0)` for the rest
  of the context. That one frame draws against stale depth.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests** in `test_glshim_band.c`. Each draws
  a scene once with `glshim_set_banding(0)` and once with banding on, from
  `srandom(1)`, and asserts `TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_MEMORY` on the canvas:
  - `test_a_held_frame_of_overlapping_lit_triangles_matches_direct`
    (depth test, smooth shading, two lights).
  - `test_a_held_frame_with_flat_shading_matches_direct`.
  - `test_a_held_frame_with_additive_blending_matches_direct`
    (`GL_ONE, GL_ONE`, depth test off).
  - `test_a_held_frame_with_polygon_offset_matches_direct`.
  - `test_a_triangle_on_a_band_boundary_matches_direct` (rows 31 and 32).
  - `test_three_frames_of_a_moving_triangle_match_direct` (the erased box).
  - `test_a_frame_that_overflows_the_store_matches_direct`
    (`glshim_band_set_capacity(4)`, 20 triangles).
  - `test_a_frame_without_a_clear_draws_directly` (assert
    `glshim_band_holding() == 0` after drawing).
  - `test_text_in_a_held_frame_lands_over_earlier_triangles` (Review Focus 4).
  - `test_a_colour_only_clear_with_depth_on_after_a_held_frame_stops_banding`
    (Review Focus 1: the frame after that one matches direct).
  - `test_banding_stays_off_when_internal_ram_is_short` (a test hook that makes
    the next band allocation fail; frames still match direct; Review Focus 2).
  - `test_closing_mid_frame_drops_the_held_calls` (clear, draw, close, open,
    swap: canvas unchanged by the old calls; Review Focus 3).
  - `test_opening_and_closing_fifty_times_does_not_grow_memory`
    (`__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`; Review Focus 5).
- [ ] **Step 2: Run them and watch them fail** (`-f test_glshim_band`).
- [ ] **Step 3: Implement** `glshim_band.c` and the `glshim.c` hooks, then
  patch the fill calls in `gl_draw_triangle_fill_plain` (`clip.c`) through
  `tinygl_patch.py` to `if (!glshim_band_fill(c->zb, fn, a, b, c)) fn(...)`,
  and add `glshim_band_spill` before `ztext.c`'s pixel write and in
  `glopDrawPixels`.
- [ ] **Step 4: Run all host tests.** Expected: all pass, and every pinned
  frame hash unchanged (held frames are exact).
- [ ] **Step 5: Mutation-check:** skip the erased box in the copy; skip the
  clear of a band; drop the y translation; skip the stale-depth switch-off;

- [ ] **Step 6: Build for the board** (`pio run -e stopwatch`) and note the
  free internal heap in the `run` line once flashed.
- [ ] **Step 7: A/B on the board** against `feature/43-gl-speed-experiments`,

- [ ] **Step 8: Commit,** with the table in the message.

### Task 4: Lines and points in held frames

**Files:**

- Modify: `firmware/src/glshim/glshim_band.h`, `glshim_band.c`
- Modify: `tools/tinygl_patch.py` (line and point call sites in `clip.c`'s

**Interfaces:**

- Consumes: Task 3's record, state table and replay.
- Produces:

```c

int glshim_band_line(ZBuffer *zb, GlshimLineFn fn, ZBufferPoint *a,

```

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests** (direct against held, exact):

- [ ] **Step 4: Run all host tests.** Expected: all pass, hashes unchanged.
- [ ] **Step 5: Mutation-check:** drop `fx`/`fy` from the record; drop the

- [ ] **Step 6: A/B on the board** as in Task 3, Step 7. Expected: Unknown

- [ ] **Step 7: Ask Rod to look** at Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel, pinned.

### Task 5: A correct, faster additive blend

**Files:**

- Modify: `tools/tinygl_patch.py` (the `GL_ONE, GL_ONE` path)
- Test: `firmware/test/test_glshim/test_glshim.c`, `test_hacks.c` hashes

**Interfaces:**

- Produces: `static inline PIXEL glshim_add565(PIXEL dst, PIXEL src)`, a
  per-channel saturating add on the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565, used
  wherever TinyGL would apply `GL_ONE, GL_ONE` with `GL_FUNC_ADD`. TinyGL's

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing tests:**

I've written the plan, and it's pushed on `feature/43-banded-renderer`:

- Locally: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-11-banded-renderer.md`

**One change from the design, for the better:** primitives are stored at the point where TinyGL calls its rasterisers, after clipping, culling, lighting and polygon offset. Replaying them per band therefore runs TinyGL's own rasterisers on the same inputs, so a banded frame should match a direct one pixel for pixel. The tests compare exactly, which is stricter than the tolerance in the design. The pinned frame hashes should only change where Task 5 deliberately fixes the additive blend's colours.

**The tasks**, with the points where you look:

1. **Hypnowheel in single precision**, registered only under a `-DHYPNOWHEEL_PROBE` build flag. Profile it; **you look**.
2. **Rasterisers kept inside a band:** three small TinyGL patches. No pixel changes.
3. **Held frames for triangles:**
   - Storage: 64-byte records in PSRAM, with a row-range table and one 32-row band in internal RAM, about 124 KB.
   - Spill and fallback when a frame can't be held, and banding switches off if internal RAM is short.
   - Exact tests against direct drawing, then an A/B of every GL hack on the board.
4. **Lines and points held too:** this is where Unknown Pleasures should speed up. A/B again; **you look** at Unknown Pleasures and Hypnowheel.
5. **The faster additive blend from #73.** It also fixes TinyGL's wrong colours for additive blending, so Hypnowheel's colours will change; **you look**.
6. **Half resolution for Hypnowheel**, flashed side by side with full resolution; **you choose**.
7. **Hypnowheel back in the rotation if you want it**, gotchas, reflash `main`, draft PR.

**Review Focus** lists five risks no ordinary test covers, each now with its own test:
- a colour-only clear after a held frame, which leaves stale depth
- internal RAM unavailable when a GL hack starts
- a hack stopped between its clear and its swap
- text drawn into a held frame
- repeated starts leaking memory

**How to run it.** I recommend **Native**: I implement every task in this session, then one fresh reviewer checks the whole branch. The tasks build tightly on one another's interfaces (the record and replay from Task 3 carry Tasks 4 to 6), and four of the seven stop for you to look at the board. Fresh agents would each have to rebuild the board and measurement context. The alternative is **Subagent-driven**: a fresh agent per task, each checked by a fresh reviewer. It's more thorough, but slower and costlier here.

# Executing Plans

Execute the plan yourself, task by task, in this session: no implementer
subagent per task, no reviewer per task. One fresh-context review of the
whole branch at the end.

**Why inline:** Subagent-driven development pays for a fresh implementer
and a fresh reviewer on every task, each re-reading the codebase from zero.
Inline execution pays for one context (yours) plus one reviewer at the end.
What it gives up is a fresh context per task and a second pair of eyes per
task. This skill keeps what those two things bought, by other means: the
brief is the spec, the ledger is your memory, TDD is the per-task gate, and
the final reviewer is the second pair of eyes.

**Core principle:** The plan already did the thinking. Execute it exactly,
prove each step with a test you watched fail and then pass, and leave a
record that survives your own forgetting.

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner
between tasks. They chose inline execution to spend less, not to answer
"should I continue?" after every task. Execute all tasks from the plan
without stopping.

**Rulings, not stalls.** Conflicts, ambiguities, plan defects — decide them.
The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger
as `Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. Deviating from the plan without a ledgered ruling is a decision made
in secret.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For
those, stop and ask.

## When to Use

- You have a plan from superpowers:writing-plans and your human partner
  chose inline execution at the handoff.
- Your harness has no subagent tool (see the per-platform references in
  `../using-superpowers/references/`). Never fabricate a dispatch; run
  the plan here.
- Tasks are mostly independent — the same precondition as
  superpowers:subagent-driven-development.

A fully specified plan makes inline execution transcription plus testing:
it runs well on a mid-tier session model, and the one place the most
capable model earns its cost is the final review, which this skill
dispatches separately. Tell your human partner so when they choose inline.

Prefer superpowers:subagent-driven-development when your human partner
wants a review gate on every task, or when the plan is long enough that
its later tasks would run on a compacted context. Inline execution over a
long plan still works — the ledger is what makes it recoverable — but the
last tasks get the least of you.

## The Process

```dot

    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {

        "task-start: brief + BASE; read the brief" [shape=box];

        "Commit as the plan's commit steps say" [shape=box];
        "Completion contract met?" [shape=diamond];

    }

    "Setup: worktree, workspace + ledger, read plan + spec, pre-flight scan" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Final whole-branch review (fresh reviewer if you have one)" [shape=box];

    "Completion contract met?" -> "Work the steps in order: TDD, run every verification, read every output" [label="no - finish the task"];

```

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. An inline executor that
loses its place re-implements tasks whose commits already exist — the same
failure as a controller re-dispatching them, paid for in your own context.
Track progress in a ledger file, not only in todos. Harness todos are a
live view; the ledger is the record.

The workspace and ledger are shared with superpowers:subagent-driven-development
— same directory, same format — so a plan can change executors mid-flight
and the new one resumes from the same ledger.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run
  `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it
  prints the plan's git-ignored directory
  (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to every
  artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, review packages. Another plan's
  directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are
  DONE — do not redo them; resume at the first task without one. Their
  commits exist in git even when your context no longer remembers making
  them: after compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own
  recollection. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file is
  another plan's progress: leave it and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch);
  if that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** load superpowers:test-driven-development now,
before Task 1. It governs every step of every task below; a plan whose
steps already say "write the failing test first" does not exempt you
from reading it.

Before Task 1, scan the plan for conflicts between tasks. The plan's
Interfaces blocks tell you where to look: for every task that consumes
what an earlier task produces, one ledger row — the two tasks, what one
produces against what the other consumes, and what you found. Tasks that
share nothing get no row; a plan whose tasks share nothing gets the single
line `Pre-flight: no shared interfaces`. Rule on each conflict a row
surfaces with the spec as the binding authority, record the ruling beside
its row, and start Task 1. Each task's own text is checked when you read
its brief, not here.

## The Task Loop

Everything you print, and every tool result, stays resident in your
context for the rest of the session. Redirect long test output to a file
in the workspace and read its tail; read a brief, not the whole plan.

### 1. Take the task

- Run this skill's `scripts/task-start PLAN_FILE N`. It prints the brief
  path and BASE (the commit the task's range is cut from) in one call.
  Read the brief for every task, including ones you remember from setup:
  what you remember is a summary, the brief has the exact values,
  signatures, and test cases.
- Mark the task's todo in_progress.

Every tool call is a turn that re-reads your whole context. Bookkeeping
rides along with work — a ledger append in the same call as the commit,
never in a call of its own.

### 2. Work the steps

The plan's steps are already in RED-GREEN order; follow them in that
order under superpowers:test-driven-development, loaded at setup. A test
step's code is written first and run first. Watching it fail is a step,
not a formality — a test that passes before the implementation exists is
a finding about the test.

Every step that runs a command has an `Expected:` line. Run the command,
read its output, and compare. Three outcomes:

- **Matches.** Next step.
- **The code is wrong.** Use superpowers:systematic-debugging. Find the
  cause; never patch the symptom to make the step's output match.
- **The plan is wrong** — a step contradicts the spec, an interface from an
  earlier task doesn't match what this task consumes, a command that
  cannot work. Rule on the smallest change that satisfies the spec, ledger
  it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`, and
  continue. The ruling is carried, not remembered: later tasks that touch
  the same interface read it from the ledger.

Commit as the plan's commit steps say. A task that spans several commits
is fine; BASE is what the review range is cut from, never `HEAD~1`.

### 3. The completion contract

Before a task's ledger line, all of the following are true, with evidence
in this session — not inferred from the diff looking right:

- Every test the brief names exists and ran in this task, and you read
  the output.
- The final test run for the task passed — `task-done` is that run, and
  it writes the command and result into the ledger line.
- Every `Expected:` line in the brief was compared against real output.
- Every deviation from the brief has a `Ruling:` line in the ledger.

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** superpowers:verification-before-completion governs
the claim. If any item is missing, the task is not complete: finish it.

### 4. Complete the task

Run this skill's `scripts/task-done PLAN_FILE N BASE -- <test command>`
with the test command the brief names for the whole task. It runs the
tests, keeps the full output in the workspace, prints the tail, and — only
if they pass — appends the completion line to the ledger:

`Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, tests: <command> → <result>)`

A failing run records nothing; the task is not complete. When it records,
mark the todo complete and take the next task.

## Final Review

Run `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD`
(MERGE_BASE = the commit the branch started from, e.g.
`git merge-base main HEAD`) and review from the file it prints.

**With a subagent tool:** dispatch the reviewer on the most capable
available model — the whole-branch review is a judgment task — using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md), with the
package path, the plan and spec paths, the plan's Review Focus section
verbatim if it has one (the input classes and failure modes the plan's
tests do not exercise — the reviewer checks each deliberately), and a
pointer to the ledger's `Ruling:` lines so it can weigh the calls you
made. Specify the model
explicitly; an omitted model inherits the session's, which may not be the
most capable. This is the one fresh context the whole run buys. Do not
skip it, and do not replace it with your own read of the diff.

**Without a subagent tool:** read code-reviewer.md and perform that review
yourself against the package, as a separate pass after the last task's
ledger line. Write `Final review: self-review (no subagent tool)` to the
ledger, and say so in your final message: a self-review by the author is
weaker than a fresh reviewer, and your human partner decides whether that
is enough before merge.

Sort the findings before you act on any of them. The reviewer's severity
labels are advice; the gate is yours. Its "Declined to judge" list is
yours too: every line there is a ruling you make and ledger, exactly like
a plan conflict — `Final: Ruling: <behavior the reviewer set aside> —
<what a reasonable person using this software gets, and why that stands
or why it is now a finding> — <cost if wrong>`. Re-grade first, by effect: the
spec is a vision document, and a finding's grade is what a reasonable
person using this software gets if it ships, not whether the spec names
the input that triggers it — a reviewer who set a finding at Minor
because the spec was silent has graded the spec, not the effect. Then:

- **Critical and Important** enter the fix pass.
- **Minor** goes to the ledger as `Final: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`
  and to your final message under "Deferred minors". Minors never enter
  the fix pass, and never become rulings — a ruling is a decision about a
  conflict, not a note that you declined a polish suggestion.

Fix the Critical and Important findings yourself — you are the
implementer here — in ONE pass. Each fix is verified by TDD, not by a
second reviewer: write the test that reproduces the finding, watch it
fail, make it pass, then run the whole suite. Record each in the ledger as
`Final: fixed <finding> — <test name> RED→GREEN, suite <N>/<N>`. A fix
without a test that failed first is not verified; a suite that is not
green after the pass means the pass is not over. Do not dispatch a
re-review: it would re-read a diff whose covering tests already answer
"addressed" and whose suite run already answers "broke nothing".

A finding you decide not to fix is a ruling — `Final: Ruling: <finding> —
<why the code stands> — <cost if wrong>` — and reaches your human partner
in the rulings list. There is no second fix pass.

## Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing
`Ruling:` into your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you
made them, each with what it costs if wrong, and every `minor (deferred)`
line under "Deferred minors". Both lists are exhaustive. Your final
message is the only place the decisions you took on your human partner's
behalf — and the findings you chose not to act on — reach them.

When the final review is clean and its fixes are committed, delete this
plan's workspace directory — the git history is the record now. Sibling
directories belong to other plans; leave them alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "I remember what Task N says" | You remember a summary. The brief has the exact values. Read it. |
| "The plan's code is right, skip watching the test fail" | A test you never saw fail proves nothing. It is one step. Run it. |
| "I'll run the full suite at the end instead of per step" | Per-step runs are how you learn which step broke it. The end-of-task run is the contract, not a substitute. |
| "The plan is wrong here, I'll just do the right thing" | Do the right thing and ledger the ruling. Unledgered deviation is a decision made in secret. |
| "I'll write the ledger lines after a few tasks" | Compaction does not wait for a convenient moment. One line per task, in the same message as the commit. |
| "Let me check in before the next task" | They chose inline to spend less. Progress prompts spend their time instead. Only the four stops stop you. |
| "I read my own diff carefully; the final reviewer is redundant" | Same author, same blind spots. The reviewer is the only fresh context this run buys. |
| "Tests should pass, the change was trivial" | "Should" is not evidence. The contract requires the command and its output. |
| "Subagents are slow and expensive, I'll skip the final review too" | Inline already removed the per-task reviewers. One review of the whole branch is the floor, not the ceiling. |
| "The reviewer said Minor, so it's Minor" | The label graded the spec's silence. Grade what the person gets. Re-grade, then gate. |
| "The fix is obvious, no need for a failing test first" | The failing test is the only proof the finding was real and is now gone. Without it you have a diff and a hope. |
| "I'll fix the minors too while I'm in there" | Every minor you fix is a test, a fix, and a suite run your partner did not ask for. Ledger them; your partner decides. |

## Example Workflow

[task-start plan 2 → brief read; BASE d4e5f6a]
[Step 2: run failing test — FAIL, but on an import error: Task 1 exported

...

[After all tasks: review-package plan MERGE_BASE HEAD; dispatch code-reviewer, most capable model]
Reviewer: One Important finding — progress reporting interval hardcoded. Two Minor.
